blocks.text: A market woman in Bodija who priced a paint-rubber of rice at ₦1,200 last harvest may be asking far more this year for the same measure. Her customers call it 'the price of everything going up'. Economists call a sustained rise in the general price level inflation — and they insist on measuring it with a basket, not with one stall.

blocks.title: Inflation
blocks.text: A sustained and appreciable rise in the general price level, which reduces the purchasing power of money. A one-off jump in the price of petrol is not inflation until it feeds through into a continuing rise across a wide basket of goods. Deflation is a sustained fall in the general price level.

rows: A slow, single-digit rise; often regarded as manageable
A faster, still moderate rise that begins to disturb planning
A rapid, usually double-digit rise that disrupts contracts
An extreme rise in which prices may change daily and money almost ceases to store value
Aggregate demand outruns aggregate supply — 'too much money chasing too few goods'
Rising wages, imported inputs or a weaker naira push firms' costs, and prices, up
Bottlenecks, poor storage, or dearer foreign goods feeding into local prices
blocks.caption: Classify inflation twice in an exam: first by how fast prices rise, then by what starts the rise

blocks.markdown:
In Nigeria, demand-pull pressure can come from large government spending financed by creating naira, or from a credit boom. Cost-push pressure often starts with a rise in the pump price of fuel, a jump in the naira price of imported wheat and machinery after depreciation, or a wage round. Structural inflation reflects poor power supply, bad roads and post-harvest losses that keep food supply inelastic. These causes can operate together.

**Do not treat a newspaper headline as a syllabus fact.** Exam calculations always give you the index numbers. Use those numbers; do not import a claimed 'current official rate' from memory.

blocks.title: A simple weighted price index and the inflation rate
blocks.prompt: A hypothetical household basket has three items. In the base year, rice costs ₦200 (weight 4), beans ₦300 (weight 2) and vegetable oil ₦500 (weight 4). In the current year the same items cost ₦250, ₦330 and ₦600. Taking the base-year index as 100, compute the current price index and the inflation rate over the period.

steps.text: Convert each price to a price relative (current ÷ base × 100).
Multiply each relative by its weight and add.
Divide by the sum of the weights, which is 10.
Inflation rate is the percentage change in the index from the base of 100.
The same 20 per cent would be described as walking or galloping depending on whether it occurred over several years or in a single year — the index tells you the size, not the label by itself.

items: **Debtors gain** — they repay a loan with naira that buy less than when they borrowed, so the real burden of the debt falls. The Federal Government, a large debtor, is among the gainers.
**Creditors and savers lose** — the real value of naira deposits, bonds and money lent is eroded.
**Fixed-income earners lose** — pensioners and workers whose wages lag behind prices can buy less.
**Producers with sticky costs may gain** in the short run if selling prices rise faster than wages and rents.
**Holders of real assets** (land, buildings, foreign currency, inventories) are relatively protected.
**Uncertainty rises** — firms postpone investment, and resources are wasted on hedging rather than production.

blocks.markdown:
### Controlling inflation

**Monetary measures** work on the money supply and the cost of credit. The CBN can raise the MPR, raise the CRR, sell securities in OMO, and call for special deposits, all of which make borrowing dearer and reduce demand-pull pressure.

**Fiscal measures** work on the budget. Government can cut recurrent spending, postpone some capital projects, and raise taxes so that a deficit shrinks or turns into a surplus. That withdraws purchasing power.

Supporting policies include raising domestic food and fuel supply, liberalising imports of scarce essentials, and incomes policies that slow wage–price spirals. Price controls without extra supply usually produce queues and black markets rather than lasting stability.

blocks.title: Write the formula before you substitute
blocks.text: Inflation rate $= \dfrac{\text{current index} - \text{previous index}}{\text{previous index}} \times 100$. A common error is to subtract from 100 when the previous index is not 100, or to divide by the current index. Another is to call any price rise 'hyperinflation' — reserve that word for an extreme collapse of the currency's store-of-value function.

points: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level; it is classified by rate (creeping, walking, galloping, hyper) and by cause (demand-pull, cost-push, structural or imported).
A price index compares the cost of a basket with a base year; the inflation rate is the percentage change in that index.
Debtors and the government as a borrower tend to gain; creditors, savers and fixed-income earners tend to lose.
Monetary control uses CRR, MPR and OMO; fiscal control uses tax increases and spending cuts.
Always compute from the figures given in the question; do not quote an unofficial 'current rate' as a fact.
